chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Jaroud, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Muslims were exhausted in Khaybar, so the Muslims hastened with their animals (to slaughter them). So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ordered them to restrain the cooking-pots (from the animals), and he did not say that they were prohibited (حرام), and that was for the preservation of the animals.'

key_terms.إِكْفَاءِ الْقُدُورِ: Restraint of the cooking-pots (stopping the cooking)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between temporary preservation and permanent prohibition regarding the meat of beasts of burden in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the pragmatic flexibility in Islamic jurisprudence during the Battle of Khaybar, where the Prophet (peace be upon him) permitted the consumption of beast of burden meat to sustain the exhausted troops. Notably, he ordered the cooking to be stopped not because the meat was inherently haram, but to preserve the animals for future utility, illustrating the distinction between temporary necessity (darurah) and permanent prohibition. This incident is frequently cited by Shia scholars to demonstrate that the meat of camels and other working animals is permissible when needed, countering views that strictly forbid it.
